title: Iranian Hackers Turn Microsoft 365 Calendar Invites Into Covert Spy Channels With HollowGraph Malware
excerpt: The sophisticated malware hides commands inside calendar events dated for 2050 and uses Microsoft's own cloud infrastructure to phone home, making detection exceptionally difficult.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • HollowGraph malware uses Microsoft 365 calendar invites for covert command and data exfiltration.
  • Commands are hidden in calendar events set for May 13, 2050, using encrypted attachments.
  • At least 12 systems infected; three were actively communicating with attackers recently.
  • The campaign is linked to Iranian threat actors targeting organizations in Israel.
  • Cybersecurity measures should focus on monitoring Microsoft Graph for unusual calendar activity.

Group-IB research report
  • A new malware module called HollowGraph uses compromised Microsoft 365 mailboxes to receive commands and exfiltrate stolen data through calendar events
  • Commands are concealed within calendar entries dated May 13, 2050, using encrypted file attachments
  • At least 12 systems have been infected, with three actively communicating with attackers between June 3 and July 9
  • Cybersecurity firm Group-IB links the campaign to an Iranian threat actor, with targets focused on organisations in Israel

Cybersecurity researchers have uncovered a sophisticated espionage campaign that repurposes one of the most mundane features of corporate life — the calendar invite — into a covert channel for malware communication. The malware, dubbed HollowGraph, uses compromised Microsoft 365 accounts to send and receive commands through calendar events, effectively turning Microsoft's own trusted cloud infrastructure against its users.

How HollowGraph Works

According to a report from cybersecurity firm Group-IB, HollowGraph authenticates to the Microsoft Graph API using hardcoded credentials from a compromised Microsoft 365 account. Its configuration file, disguised as a regular log file named "logAzure.txt," contains tenant IDs, client secrets, mailbox addresses, and RSA encryption keys.

https://x.com/The_Cyber_News/status/2079258799693795603

The malware creates calendar events dated May 13, 2050 — far enough in the future that they are unlikely to be noticed during routine calendar use. Commands and stolen data are concealed within encrypted file attachments on these entries. HollowGraph retrieves new instructions by searching for events within a fixed one-hour window between 22:00 and 23:00 UTC on that future date.

"HOLLOWGRAPH demonstrates a high level of technical sophistication. Its use of trusted cloud infrastructure for command-and-control, hybrid encryption, and DNS tunneling collectively suggest significant technical capabilities and operational maturity."

— Group-IB research report

The Iran Connection

Group-IB's analysis identified technical similarities with Lyceum, an Iranian-nexus threat actor, though researchers cautioned that the available evidence is insufficient for high-confidence attribution. What is clear is the campaign's focus: all collected indicators point to targeted attacks on organisations in Israel, suggesting an espionage operation.

Targeted Espionage Campaign
›Linked to Iranian threat actor Lyceum.
›Focus on organizations in Israel.
›Utilizes Microsoft Graph API for communication.
›Employs hybrid encryption and DNS tunneling.
https://youtube.com/watch?v=AOQETNsmTEU

At least 12 systems have been infected with HollowGraph, with three actively communicating with the threat actor between June 3 and July 9, 2026.

Why It Matters

The attack highlights a growing trend in cybersecurity: adversaries leveraging trusted cloud services to evade detection. Because the malware communicates entirely through Microsoft Graph API — a legitimate Microsoft service used by millions of organisations worldwide — traditional network monitoring tools are unlikely to flag the traffic as suspicious.

HollowGraph also maintains a backup DNS tunnelling channel through an attacker-controlled domain, used to refresh authentication credentials. Each returned IPv6 address yields 14 usable payload bytes, which the malware assembles and decodes as UTF-8 text.

What Organisations Should Do

Group-IB recommends that security teams monitor Microsoft Graph and Microsoft 365 audit logs for suspicious application-driven calendar activity — particularly events set far in the future with unusual subjects or attachments. Organisations should also enforce Conditional Access policies, restrict and audit OAuth client-credential applications, and monitor outbound DNS for tunnelling patterns.

For the millions of Indian IT professionals who administer Microsoft 365 environments globally, the discovery underscores the need to treat calendar infrastructure as a potential attack surface, not just a productivity tool.
